paper_metadata.title: Quantum Risk Analysis of Financial Derivatives

experiments.description: Numerical simulation of the QAE-based VaR algorithm for derivative portfolios, comparing estimated VaR error versus oracle calls and amplitude-estimation accuracy on sampled scenario prices.

algorithm.variant: QAE-based VaR estimation with coherent inner QAE and outer QAE bisection search
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Bisection search stops when 1 - alpha is contained in the QAE confidence interval [pl, ph] for the current threshold candidate.

problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate VaR of a derivative portfolio by finding the smallest threshold mu such that P[V <= mu] >= 1 - alpha, where V is the portfolio value across scenarios.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic portfolio-value scenarios drawn from a normal distribution and used to simulate VaR estimation.

dataset_specification.description: Scenario prices sampled from N(mu=0.5, sigma^2=0.09^2); 100 independent samples per data point.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: For each sample, generate N=5000 scenario prices from the normal distribution and compute the classical VaR estimate by sorting prices and taking the 1-alpha percentile.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute absolute error between quantum VaR estimate and classical VaR estimate; average over 100 independent samples.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical nested Monte Carlo VaR estimation
speedup_claims.conditions: when derivative pricing itself is done with Monte Carlo and the QAE-based inner pricing step is used
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the QAE-based VaR method has the same asymptotic scaling as the classical nested Monte Carlo approach up to the quadratic speedup from amplitude estimation; no explicit numerical speedup factor is reported for this experiment.

experiments.description: Numerical simulation of the QSP-based VaR algorithm for derivative portfolios, comparing estimated VaR error versus oracle calls and amplitude-estimation accuracy on sampled scenario prices.

algorithm.variant: QSP-based VaR estimation with polynomial threshold approximation and outer QAE bisection search
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Bisection search stops when 1 - alpha is contained in the QAE confidence interval [pl, ph] for the current threshold candidate.

problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate VaR of a derivative portfolio by finding the smallest threshold mu such that P[V <= mu] >= 1 - alpha, using a QSP polynomial approximation to the threshold function.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic portfolio-value scenarios drawn from a normal distribution and used to simulate QSP-based VaR estimation.

dataset_specification.description: Scenario prices sampled from N(mu=0.5, sigma^2=0.09^2); 100 independent samples per data point.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: For each sample, generate N=5000 scenario prices from the normal distribution and compute the classical VaR estimate by sorting prices and taking the 1-alpha percentile.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute absolute error between quantum VaR estimate and classical VaR estimate; average over 100 independent samples.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical nested Monte Carlo VaR estimation
speedup_claims.conditions: when using QSP to approximate the threshold function and QAE for readout
speedup_claims.caveats: Asymptotically the QSP-based method has the same scaling as the QAE-based method, but with fewer quantum resources; no explicit numerical speedup factor is reported for this experiment.

experiments.description: Resource comparison between QAE-based and QSP-based VaR estimation, measuring oracle-call counts required to reach a target VaR error under sampled normal scenario prices.

algorithm.variant: QAE VaR versus QSP VaR resource comparison
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Bisection search with stopping condition 1 - alpha in the estimated confidence interval; resource comparison performed at matched VaR error.

problem_formulation.objective_function: Compare the number of oracle invocations needed by QAE and QSP to estimate VaR of a derivative portfolio to the same accuracy.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic scenario prices sampled from a normal distribution; same setup used to compare QAE and QSP oracle-call efficiency.

dataset_specification.description: Scenario prices sampled from N(mu=0.5, sigma^2=0.09^2); 100 independent samples per data point.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical VaR estimate obtained by sorting sampled scenario prices and taking the 1-alpha percentile.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Average absolute VaR error across 100 samples; compare oracle-call counts for QAE and QSP.

results.unit: oracle calls per QAE oracle call pair baseline not directly comparable
oracle calls per QAE oracle call pair baseline not directly comparable
approximate empirical reduction factor in oracle calls for QSP vs QAE

speedup_claims.conditions: for the sampled normal scenario-price benchmark with N=5000, alpha=0.99, and epsilon_A in {1e-4, 5e-4}
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports this as an average over 100 independent samples and notes the advantage is observed over the error range examined.

speedup_claims.conditions: asymptotically, both QAE and QSP VaR methods scale similarly in the number of oracle calls needed for a target accuracy
speedup_claims.caveats: QSP has significantly fewer quantum resources for the same target accuracy, but the asymptotic scaling is the same.

experiments.description: Quantum-advantage benchmark for QSP-based VaR estimation on an autocallable derivative, estimating the logical QPU clock rate required to match classical runtime as a function of scenario-preparation T-depth.

algorithm.convergence_criteria: Search over polynomial degree d and QAE accuracy epsilon_A until quantum VaR error matches classical VaR error.

problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate VaR of an autocallable derivative portfolio and compare quantum and classical end-to-end runtime at matched estimation error.

problem_instance.description: Autocallable derivative product benchmark from prior work, with scenario prices drawn from a normal distribution.

dataset_specification.description: Autocallable derivative product studied in Ref. [6]; scenario prices modeled as normal N(mu, sigma^2) with sigma=0.09 and mu averaged over {0.45, 0.48, 0.5, 0.52, 0.55} for the quantum benchmark.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical benchmark prices N scenarios in one second each, then sorts simulated prices to estimate VaR.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute classical VaR error relative to the normal-distribution quantile; repeat 200 times and use the standard deviation of errors as classical error metric.

results.unit: VaR error relative to normal-distribution quantile

classical_baselines.unit: VaR error relative to normal-distribution quantile

speedup_claims.factor: up to about 30x lower logical clock rate required for quantum advantage
speedup_claims.baseline_method: single-derivative pricing quantum advantage threshold from Ref. [19]
speedup_claims.conditions: for N = 50000 scenarios and sufficiently low scenario-preparation T-depth (approximately TS ≲ 3 × 10^5)
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a benchmarked estimate based on simulated scenario prices and resource modeling, not a hardware demonstration.

speedup_claims.factor: QSP VaR requires advantage threshold TS ≲ 8 × 10^7 for N = 50000
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical runtime for pricing N scenarios in N seconds
speedup_claims.conditions: for the autocallable benchmark with N = 50000 scenarios
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a threshold on scenario-preparation T-depth, not a direct speedup factor.

speedup_claims.conditions: when comparing QSP-based VaR to classical nested Monte Carlo under the same scenario-sampling assumptions
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper frames the advantage in terms of reduced logical clock rate and asymptotic scaling; actual advantage depends strongly on scenario preparation cost.
